The gaze, the mirror and representation of a self in the treatment of a young boy with pervasive developmental delay and marked autistic features

Vijé Franchi

Vijé Franchi

Geneva 4
Switzerland
Faculty of Psychology and Educational Sciences

Vijé Franchi   *Email: vije.franchi@gmail.com
autistic states, mirror, mirroring, self, traumatic disillusionment, infantile transference

This paper explores the ways in which the ‘recognition of a self’ aspect of mirroring, as epitomised by the mother’s gaze of her newborn at the breast, served to set development in motion in the case of Adam, a little boy of four and a half, who was referred for psychotherapy after receiving a diagnosis of pervasive developmental delay with marked autistic features. The paper uses detailed clinical material to track Adam’s development of a representation of his self and his object and his use of the mirror in this process. The author shows how Adam went from not recognising his reflection in the mirror to seeing the reflection of himself in the therapist’s eyes and then using the mirror to support his exploration and internalisation of the permanence of his self and his objects as well as their physical and psychic characteristics and functions. The author also seeks to demonstrate ways in which Adam’s use of the mirror facilitated emotional engagement and working through of painful aspects of the infantile transference: these included primitive anxieties related to being seen and taken into the mind by the object; feelings of terror and loss inherent in experiencing the self and the object as separate; and intense rivalry and envy of the other occupants of the object’s mind. Lastly, the author seeks to show how Adam’s work at the mirror linked to the emergence of verbal language and the development of symbolic thinking.

The excerpt opens with some key details of the patient’s history giving a helpful context to generate some first ideas about this young woman’s difficulties and also the details of the presented session. We learn that Lily comes from a professional family with expectations of high academic achievement. As her mother is a general practitioner, it is likely that the family culture includes a familiarity with and interest in the manifest changes, the signs and symptoms of the body. The corporeal self is in focus and perhaps, with this, ideas about ‘health’ are more defined in this family.

Lily is attending her sixth session, perhaps her ninth meeting with her therapist. I would regard this as still early in their relationship, though not too soon for powerful emotional exchanges to take place. We learn that Lily has been referred for psychotherapy after being discharged from hospital where her treatment has involved very invasive, uncompromising contact with her body, in response to the severity of her symptoms of anorexia. It sounds as if the patient, like other young people afflicted with an eating disorder, has found some kind of refuge, or displacement, for intolerable emotional states in somatic expression. Not only is the body suffering from illness, but the illness demands physical treatments. Both elements of this physical experience are probably employed unconsciously to ward off the experience of psychic pain.

In this session, there is a strained atmosphere and the therapist communicates his or her bewildered sense of being coshed, rendered mindless and weak, alongside feelings of deep concern about the young patient. Much of the therapist’s experience will be recognised by those who work with troubled adolescents, especially patients with obsessional symptoms or eating disorders. Lily’s apparent passivity and fragility evoke a terrified state in the countertransference and the therapist finds herself almost embarrassed by the apparent crudeness of her own vitality and health. As they journey from the waiting room to the consulting room, the therapist has to contain a miserable sense of losing or dropping Lily as if she really is little more than the waif described.

My initial impression of this sixth session of psychotherapy is of the breathtaking contrast between 17-year-old Lily’s profound fragility and her silent steely power. This is a young woman who has suffered from life-threatening anorexia nervosa and continues to be at the mercy of anorexic states of mind. The transference/counter-transference dynamics have the familiar hallmarks of this punishing illness. The clear background summary provides a useful external perspective for considering Lily’s internal world. She has recently been discharged from hospital, has a history of poor engagement in individual work and so, at the beginning stages of Lily’s psychotherapy, there are understandable concerns about the viability of this work.

There has been a psychotherapy assessment where one imagines that Lily was able to tolerate emotional contact; that there was evidence of a part of her that might hope for change and a view formed by her therapist that there was potential to mobilise this in response to the more stuck and anti-life/anti-developmental parts of Lily. It is significant that Lily comes to these initial sessions and that in the early stages a relational experience, however rudimentary, has begun. The transference experience is rich and alive, possibly symbolised for us by the therapist in her description of Lily’s long red braided hair, a weaving together of vibrant colour amidst the drab, sad isolation of the session. In addition there is the larger than life art book of Frida Kahlo’s work which has been provided as a result of Lily letting her therapist know about her interest in this artist and her therapist’s active response of then introducing the book into the psychotherapy to create a third space.

The close attention and minutely captured observations of Lily is reminiscent of closely observed psychoanalytic infant observation. This contrasts starkly with Lily’s gaze that seems barely to connect with her therapist. Lily’s physicality and somatic responses are telling; her fragile frame supporting a head that seems disproportionately large; the tiny aggressive shake of the head in the waiting room and the journey to the consulting room like walking on a thousand sharp knives. These physical moments evoke images of a premature baby – jerky, reflexive, hypersensitive; born too soon and ill-prepared for life. The emotional atmosphere is balanced on the cusp of life and death. Irreducibly human encounters: therapeutic alliance and treatment outcome in child and adolescent psychotherapy

Cameron M. Clark

Journal of Infant, Child & Adolescent Psychotherapy, Informa, 2013, Volume 12 (3): 228–43

Background: The concept of therapeutic alliance is examined in relation to treatment outcomes in youth psychotherapy. The first section of the article develops an intuitive account wherein the relationship between the therapist and youth client is purported to hold great significance for treatment effectiveness in psychological interventions. The remainder of the article aims to validate this deep-rooted intuition via close examination of how therapeutic alliance has been defined, measured, and meta-analysed in the current literature. Methodological and philosophical challenges to the concept and implications for future research and practice are discussed. Cautious, but optimistic conclusions are drawn affirming the intuitive position that the relationship between therapist and youth client does indeed impact treatment outcome.

Background: Using a novel approach to assess attachment to therapist from patient narratives (Patient Attachment to Therapist Rating Scale; PAT-RS), we investigated the relationships between secure attachment to therapist, patient-rated alliance, and outcome in a sample of 70 young adults treated with psychoanalytic psychotherapy. Editorial

Kate Stratton and Jo Russell

Jo Russell

Jo Russell  

This is a general edition of the Journal which once again reflects the wide range of work undertaken by child psychotherapists and the continued creative application of the profession in different settings. All of the papers presented here, from very different vantage points, approach the complex and enduring question of what enables therapeutic change: from the perspective of clinician-researcher, examining the therapeutic process and what actually takes place in the consulting room (the articles by Salomonsson and Goodman); from a clinical standpoint, exploring some familiar issues of technique with a ‘hard to reach’ patient (Della Rosa) and from the perspective of a child psychotherapist in a community outreach setting, highlighting how a psychoanalytic perspective may enable us – and our patients – to survive in uncertain times (Argent). We also have a contribution from Mary Brady which interweaves theory, literature and clinical practice and provides a striking illustration of the many diverse sources that inform and enrich our daily practice. We hope that the balance between clinical and research-oriented papers provides a stimulating read.

The edition opens with another rich and thought-provoking article by Björn Salomonsson in which he addresses the process of change in toddler–parent psychotherapy. Employing a psychoanalytically based technique that emphasises the therapist’s interaction with the child in the presence of the parent (Salomonsson, 2015), the author explores the question of how joint work with a mother and young child can influence the child, despite limitations in the toddler’s verbal understanding. Sensitive clinical material demonstrates in vivid detail the toddler’s responses to communications from both his mother and the therapist. But what, the author asks, does the child actually perceive in the therapeutic interchange, how does this affect him and how do such processes work? Salomonsson usefully integrates neuroscientific and experimental research evidence about the child’s capacities with psychoanalytic theory to consider what might be happening in the ‘therapeutic action’. While he ultimately concludes that this remains complex and elusive – ‘an unfinished puzzle’ – his attempts to clarify how the child perceives, interprets and progresses during his treatment make for compelling reading, and we hope the paper will stimulate further debate on this important subject.

Therapeutic action in psychoanalytic therapy with toddlers and parents

Björn Salomonsson

Björn Salomonsson

Stockholm
Sweden
Unit of Reproductive Health, Department of Women’s and Children’s Health

Björn Salomonsson   *Email: bjorn.salomonsson@ki.se
parent–toddler, mirror neurons, facial communication, countertransference, mother–infant psychoanalytic treatment

Psychotherapy with toddlers and parents can focus on promoting attachment, facilitating development and improving interactions. Some techniques provide guidance to the parents, whereas others interpret to them their unconscious fantasies or ‘ghosts’ contributing to the child’s disorder. A recent paper introduced a psychoanalytically oriented technique, which emphasised the therapist’s interaction with the child in the presence of the parent(s). The child was addressed about his/her unconscious motivations in the session and the feelings towards the therapist. Also, the parent’s transference onto the therapist was seen as a vehicle that might further the therapeutic process and was accordingly addressed. The present paper analyses the therapeutic action in such treatments. Whereas work with the parents resembles that of ordinary psychodynamic therapy, therapeutic action is more difficult to conceptualise regarding the toddler, whose understanding of verbal interpretations and the therapist’s dialogues with the parent is more limited than that of an adult. However, a clinical vignette demonstrates a toddler’s precise and swift reactions to communications from mother or therapist. The paper investigates evidence from neuroscience and psychological research as to which communicative channels – beyond words – toddlers might perceive and comprehend. In addition, it is claimed that the countertransference is key to explaining how the therapist understands such communication.

Donna Gillies, Fiona Taylor, Carl Grey, Louise O’Brien and Natalie D’Abrew

Background: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is highly prevalent in children and adolescents who have experienced trauma and has high personal and health costs. Although a wide range of psychological therapies have been used in the treatment of PTSD there are no systematic reviews of these therapies in children and adolescents.

Editorial

Kate Stratton and Jo Russell

Jo Russell

Jo Russell  

This issue contains a range of papers of clinical and theoretical interest, reflecting both the breadth of work undertaken by child psychotherapists and the consolidation and development of research based on accumulated clinical experience. Taken together, we hope that they succeed in conveying something of the sense of interest and excitement with which these authors have approached challenging clinical situations – with the demands they make on practitioners to re-think technique, theory and approach – and the energy that has gone into research projects that demonstrate a practice fully alive, and relevant, to the challenges and opportunities facing us as a profession. We hope, too, that the overlap of clinical, research and theoretical interests between the authors, as well as their differences, makes for a rich and stimulating read.

The first two papers, by Maria Rhode and Andrew Briggs, converge in several ways. Both explore the frontier of body and psyche and consider the sorts of powerful responses that can make us feel deeply uncomfortable but also more in touch with our patients if we are able to recognise and understand them. Rhode’s lucid, thought-provoking article addresses difficulties in the therapist’s capacity to think and to recognise meaningful patterns in work with children on the autistic spectrum. The paper explores two of the countertransference pathways that can lead to this situation, focusing on the impact of projective and adhesive identification: the extent of bodily and emotional cohesion that a child has achieved, the author suggests, exerts an important influence on which pathway may predominate. Rhode’s paper is, like the other articles in this issue, rich in clinical detail that vividly conveys the challenges of understanding and working with such children. It is particularly interesting to be able to follow her detailed thinking about the extreme bodily anxieties that, for some autistic children, can accompany the awareness of being physically separate and the ways in which these may be forcefully experienced in the bodily countertransference.

Valli Kohon

Valli Kohon

London
UK

Valli Kohon   *Email: vallishaio@kohon.co.uk

The background information reveals a very disturbed young man, with a serious history of mental illness, self-harm and suicidality. Nevertheless, he is able and functioning to the extent of having completed a university degree in mathematics and trained in accountancy. He seems to be in a demanding job, which he appears not to be managing very well.

The description of what it is like to be in the room with him sheds light on the patient’s defences: flippant humour to deflect any serious thoughts and the use of language to create a barrier, rather than to communicate. The patient reiterates: “nothing in my mind” or “nothing else”; does he have to keep his mind empty or induce the therapist to fill it for him? The empty or convoluted talk mentioned by the therapist raises the question of what that might mean for the young man: is he afraid of letting anything in, including his own thoughts? There seems to be a deep-seated anxiety about engaging in an analytic intercourse, of being penetrated by the therapist; the analytic dialogue conveys superficiality and flatness; there is a kind of externality that perhaps suggests fears regarding homosexuality.

The destructive and scathing thoughts he expresses towards others also serve defensive functions and reflect some destructive aspects of his relationship to himself.

The therapist evokes aspects of the transference relationship: awareness of being with a disturbed and disturbing patient, the experience of the patient’s flight into excitement characterised by fantasies of doing violence to others, risk-taking or self-harm. The patient’s desire to shock or unnerve the therapist with these graphic accounts reveals his aggression and a perverse wish to engage him or her in an exciting way. Together with his undermining and mocking response, the patient reflects a wish to keep his therapist under control and at a distance. According to the present account, he has said little about his parents and sibling or about important relationships; in spite of this, he provides the therapist with significant material regarding his relation to his objects.

Katie Argent is a consultant child and adolescent psychotherapist in the Fostering, Adoption and Kinship Care Team at the Tavistock and Portman NHS Foundation Trust. Mary Brady (Ph.D) is an adult, adolescent and child psychoanalyst. She is in the faculty of the San Francisco Centre for Psychoanalysis. She works in private practice in San Francisco and also co-leads a consultation group on ‘The treatment of adolescents and young adults’. Her book, The Body in Adolescence: Psychic Isolation and Physical Symptoms, will be published by Routledge in December 2015.

Elena Della Rosa is a child psychotherapist who trained at the Tavistock. She is currently working at Bexley CAMHS where she does most of her work within an Adolescent team. She is interested in issues of therapeutic technique and is writing a research doctorate on the role of transference interpretations in short-term psychotherapy with adolescents suffering from depression.

Judith Edwards (Ph.D) is a retired consultant child and adolescent psychotherapist who has taught and supervised on many courses at the Tavistock Clinic, where she has worked in various capacities since the 1980s. A past editor of the Journal of Child Psychotherapy, she has published her work in papers and academic books internationally. Apart from her clinical experience, one of her principal interests has been in the links between psychoanalysis, culture and the arts, as well as making psychoanalytic ideas accessible to a wide audience. Her memoir, Pieces of Molly: An Ordinary Life, was published by Karnac in November 2014.

Robert Fleming is a consultant child and adolescent psychotherapist with South London and Maudsley NHS Trust. Originally from Scotland, he was a social worker in South London before working in a child guidance clinic in America. He returned to the UK and trained as a child and adolescent psychotherapist at the Tavistock and later as an adult psychotherapist at the BAP (now BPF). Throughout his professional life, he has had an interest in the substitute care of children unable to live with their birth parents. He completed his doctoral research in this area.

Clinical material

Clinical material

Background

Lily is a 17-year-old young woman who has suffered from severe anorexia nervosa since her early teenage years. Lily’s health has been so compromised by her extreme food restricting that she has needed extended inpatient stays including two periods of several months being fed via a bridled naso-gastric tube. Consequently, Lily has missed a whole year of education, so that she is now just beginning her A-levels. Lily lives with her parents, who are both GPs; her mother is of Irish descent, the first and only of many siblings to go to university. Lily has twin older brothers whom she adored as a little girl; both have been highly successful academically. Lily is particularly close to one of her brothers, who suffers from mild spasticity; at one point he was the only person she would tolerate watching her eat. Several attempts have been made over the years to engage Lily in individual therapy but none has ‘taken’. The present referral was made to the local CAMHS team on Lily’s discharge from hospital four months previously. This session is the sixth of once-weekly work following a three-session assessment.

Session material

Lily is waiting with her head bowed when I go to get her from the waiting room. She looks like a refugee or a Victorian pauper in layers of drab clothing that hang off an immensely fragile frame. As I gently say her name, she looks up at me with a far away, almost bewildered expression, as though I have just called her back from a dream state. She gives a tiny yet aggressive shake of her head. I wonder to myself what thought(s) she might be trying to ‘shake off’, what world she might be having to pull herself away from? Lily rises slowly, unfolding herself. Every movement seems to take the greatest of efforts. Her head appears disproportionately large, too heavy to support and she takes small hesitant steps with the greatest of difficulty. The impression is that even the smallest of physical demands, such as the transport of her body to the therapy room, are exhaustingly painful. I am reminded of the story of the little mermaid (Anderson, 1974), for whom every step is ‘as though she were walking on a thousand sharp knives’. Our slow progress together feels like that of patients who must pull a mobile intravenous drip with them as they shuffle through a hospital ward; I feel I am having to watchfully drag her behind me, very careful not to dislodge our delicate point of connection.

Clinical material

Background

Harry is a 24-year-old man. He works as an accountant in large successful firm, having studied mathematics and applied mathematics at university. He was referred for psychotherapy due to increasing concerns, both his own and those of his managers, about his capacity to cope with the pressure of the workload. Having had a positive experience of psychotherapy in the past, as a young adolescent, it was felt that this kind of space might again be helpful to him. Harry has a significant history of mental health difficulties. He started self-harming, by cutting himself, in his early teens, and attempted suicide on a number of occasions, all of which seemed to have been heightened during particular transitional periods: from primary to senior school, college to university and now, once more, as he negotiates the beginnings of adult life.

My first impressions of Harry were of a very bright, intelligent, articulate young man who manages a deep level of disturbance and underlying fragility with a façade of humour and flippancy. He uses his intellect in a very defensive, concrete way, which often disables both of our thinking, using word games or talking in riddles that apparently say something and yet simultaneously say absolutely nothing. This seems to be Harry’s default position. However the humour and flippancy often give way to depressive thoughts about himself and his future. Harry can also reveal destructive and scathing attitudes towards others that appear to mask the more vulnerable, needy parts of himself.

Being in the room with Harry, at the beginning of his therapy, I was very aware of being with someone who was both very disturbed and disturbing. Any fleeting moments of meaningful contact between us such as making links between his behaviour and his feelings, or a collaborative sharing of ideas about what might be occurring for him on an unconscious level, were regularly displaced by perverse excitement about self-harming or risk-taking activities. On these occasions Harry would resort to undermining and mocking our work, giving me graphic reports of his cutting and detailed descriptions of violent fantasies involving harming himself and others.

Clinical commentary by Inge Gregorius, psychoanalytic psychotherapist with children, young people and adults

Harry struck me as a defended young man who struggles to put his emotions into words and tends to communicate by evoking feelings in others and acting out. It is difficult to get close to him. I couldn’t help being reminded of some of the patients I have worked with and I felt this helped and hindered me in thinking about the relationship with his therapist in this session.

This was Harry’s last session before a weekend break. In view of his apparent sensitivity to change, I could see that this was likely to be problematic. It gradually emerged that he was having to negotiate several transitions at this time. In therapy, this session came soon after the summer break and there were unresolved changes of session time. This would have been his second summer break, as he had been in this therapy for 18 months, so one would expect a reaction. According to Meltzer (1967: 12) ‘the gathering of the transference is disrupted by patterns of acting out as the main stream of transference takes shape’. At work, Harry was in presumably his first job, a highly pressured one, and had just been given a new project. It is worth noting that he seemed to be in a supportive work environment with good pastoral care and that he was encouraged to get therapeutic help.

Harry is also described as having difficulty coping with even fleeting moments of meaningful contact, which tend to leave him feeling vulnerable. He diverts from feeling this way by resorting to perverse excitement about self-harming or risk-taking activities. Again, it is to be expected that his anxieties and defences in this area will increase as the transference deepens (Meltzer, 1967: 9).

Harry seems to me to be subtly acting out in this session. Perhaps it is a mark of progress in the therapy that there is not more overt acting out. Harry could bring the troubling issues into the session through discussing difficulties at work, through his way of relating to his therapist and the feelings he evokes in his therapist and through the dream he brings. Perhaps, Harry is also protecting his therapist, as the therapist suggests Harry-in-the-dream does with the woman.

[[RunningHead]]

Research digest: reflective function

Introduction

This Research Digest is focused on the current and potential use of Reflective Function (RF) as a research method. RF is intended to be a method of measuring the capacity for mentalizing, both in the moment and across a longer time period. It is generally applied to semi-structured research interviews, such as the well-known Adult Attachment Interview (AAI) and the Parent Development Interview (PDI), and there is increasing interest in applying it to researching clinical sessions (for example, Goodman, 2013). The first abstract in this Digest is from 2005 (Fonagy and Target) and we have included it because it sets the scene with the idea that the transmission of attachment status from parent to child is, in part at least, carried out through parental mentalizing and RF. The second abstract (Katznelson, 2014) presents a review of the research that has taken place in this field since, including the association between RF and other measures, and covers both parental mentalizing and mentalizing in psychiatric populations. Readers of this journal with a particular interest in infancy and parent–infant attachment may note Stacks et al. (2014), Ensink et al. (2014) and Berthelot et al. (2015). RF in fathers is explored in Benbassat and Priel (2015) and Smith Stover and Kiselica (2014). Clinicians with an interest in adolescence may note Ha et al. (2013), Borelli et al. (2015) and Möller et al. (2015). Developments in RF research tools for diverse populations are described in, for example, Ensink et al. (2014 – pregnant women with a history of trauma) and Pajulo et al. (2015 – prenatal parents). The original hypothesis from 2005 is followed up in, for example, Chiesa and Fonagy (2014).

Bridging the transmission gap: an end to an important mystery of attachment research?

Peter Fonagy and Mary Target

Attachment & Human Development, Informa, 2005, Volume 7 (3): 333–43

The authors provide a context for this special section by arguing that the attachment relationships of infancy fulfil an evolutionary role in ensuring that the brain structures that come to subserve social cognition are appropriately organised and prepared to equip the individual for the collaborative existence with other people for which his or her brain was designed. Processes as fundamental as gene expression or changes in receptor densities can be seen as direct functions of the extent of understanding of mental states provided by the caregiving environment. If the attachment relationship is indeed a major organiser of brain development, it is even more important to understand the processes that underpin the transgenerational transmission of attachment patterns. The contributions of the papers in the special section to understanding the role of reflective function in the development of attachment and social cognition are reviewed, and the implications for the development of both theory and practice are explored.

Author biographies

Andrew Briggs is Trust Head of Child and Adolescent Psychotherapy at Sussex Partnership NHS Foundation Trust. He is also an organisational consultant. In both roles, he has a specialist clinical interest in children and young people in the care system. As well as seeing this vulnerable patient group in psychotherapy he has consulted within the tertiary sector to residential units, and to local authority social work managers and teams. His publications include those on difficult to reach children and the infant observation method. He has edited two books on children in care in the Karnac/Tavistock series: Waiting to be Found: Papers on Children in Care (2013) and Towards Belonging: Negotiating New Relationships for Adopted Children and Those in Care (2015).

Ricky Emanuel is a consultant child and adolescent and adult psychotherapist working at the Royal Free Hospital London and in private practice. This new book by Graham Music, hot on the heels of his excellent Nuturing Natures (Music, 2010), is a very important and timely one. As is the case with all his writing, it is saturated with bang up-to-date research evidence with a reference list covering 40 pages. How Graham reads all this and what is more absorbs essential facts is quite extraordinary given he has a day job as well. The fact he makes these studies accessible to all of us is an act of altruism in itself.

Through focussing on the ‘Good Life’, defined by Aristotle as a life lived ethically and which feels good, which we now term well-being or flourishing, the book attempts to rebalance to some extent the perceived focus psychoanalytic theories tend to have on the negative and destructive tendencies although proper reading of someone like Melanie Klein shows this not to be the case. Her famous paper, ‘Envy and gratitude’ (Klein, 1957), is remembered more for its study of envy rather than her extensive writing about gratitude or generosity. This, to me, is one of the flaws of this book as Graham seems to largely ignore or, at most, to pay passing reference to psychoanalysis when many of the studies he is illustrating largely reinforce the psychoanalytic position. The importance of this book as a social and political statement about the diminution of altruism and the rise of selfishness and narcissism in Western society is most welcome. However, at a time when psychoanalysis and psychotherapy is under such attack in the same societies, psychoanalytic thinking could have been supported and strengthened if its main tenets were shown to be underpinned by the new research studies Graham so eloquently describes and explains. As such this book misses a serious political opportunity to stand up for the bedrock of our profession. I will illustrate this point later. This one misgiving should not put off the reader from devouring this book as it is full of richness and fascinating material.

Graham convincingly challenges the discourse that ‘human beings are primarily selfish and competitive and not naturally fair and cooperative’ (p. 3). He goes on to say, ‘Much contemporary research suggests that this view of human nature is limited, and underestimates the extent to which we are born primed for altruism, cooperation and generosity’ (p. 4). Rebecca Bergese is a child and adolescent psychotherapist who trained at the Tavistock Centre and now works with children and parents in private practice; she also offers supervision and teaches on Tavistock courses in London and Belfast. She currently holds the chair of ‘Emotional and relational dimensions of education and training’ at the University of Geneva and co-directs a Master’s degree course in Early Childhood Special Needs Education. This first edition of the Journal in 2015 contains some thought-provoking and innovative ideas about working with some very challenging children and their families.

Björn Salomonsson’s paper raises some interesting technical questions about psychoanalytically informed parent–toddler therapy. The author defines his clinical approach with a detailed account of his work with a two-and-a-half-year-old boy and his depressed mother. With animated detail, he subtly traces the moment-to-moment movement within sessions as different states of mind, in both child and parent, are played out. The paper goes on to consider some key approaches to parent–toddler work, highlighting similarities and differences between models. Does Salomonsson’s approach, as the title suggests, constitute an ‘extension of the field’ of parent–toddler therapy? Is it a difference of degree or kind? Whatever the answer, Salomonsson’s overarching emphasis on ‘a dialogue with parent and child and on interpretations relating to the unconscious motivations of each of them’ allows for valuable reflection on the complex dynamics involved in parent–toddler work and will contribute to the evolving debate on technique.

Pozzi, Micotti and Rashid’s paper explores the phenomenon, little studied in psychoanalytic literature, of children with selective mutism. The paper offers a literature review followed by two case histories of children who would not speak outside of the home. The writers look at the complexity of intergenerational dysfunctional dynamics within the family, specifically around issues of trauma and loss in different forms, which it is believed contributed to the symptoms of selective mutism in the children. A variety of multi-disciplinary interventions is described: individual psychotherapy, parent–child psychotherapy and family therapy. What emerges is a picture of ‘silent’ parents and families following some unspoken emotional trauma. The clinicians helped the families to give voice to unthinkable events and emotions, freeing them to address previously paralysing thoughts. Pozzi describes her work in detail and with great sensitivity, showing how her use of the countertransference freed her when she too became paralysed in her thinking, a state she calls ‘mutism of the mind’.

This study examined the constellation of interaction structures – repetitive patterns of interactions between patient and therapist over the course of treatment – that emerged in the psychodynamic therapy (PDT) of a child diagnosed with borderline personality disorder and treated by two doctoral student therapists. Identification of these interaction structures can inform therapists of what might be expected from patients with particular symptom or behaviour patterns and how interactions change over time. This study also examined each session’s adherence to three session prototypes: PDT, cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT) and reflective functioning (RF) process. The Child Psychotherapy Q-Set (CPQ) is a 100-item instrument that assesses the processes within a single psychotherapy session. Items reflect a wide range of therapist attitudes and behaviours, patient attitudes and behaviours and interactions between therapist and patient. Experts used the CPQ to define PDT, CBT and RF process session prototypes. The results suggested that four distinct interaction structures could be identified and that their constellations differed between the two therapists and also differed over time within each treatment. Therapists were more structured and accommodating early on in their treatments and more interpretive later. Prototypical PDT process was more prominent in the sessions than RF process, which in turn was more prominent than CBT process. Unique therapeutic processes are at work in every dyad, despite holding the patient and theoretical orientation constant. An effective treatment in one dyad might not work in another due to therapist-specific and dyad-specific effects.

This paper discusses psychoanalytic witnessing as the prerequisite for psychoanalytic psychotherapy with a severely sexually traumatised young adolescent boy, Dean. This form of witnessing acted as a prior stage for treatment through the psychotherapist acknowledging Dean’s trauma, without seeking to symbolise its registration in the psychotherapeutic relationship. As sexual abuse is about something done to the person, this acknowledging crucially conveys belief in the truth of what has happened to the patient at the hands of the external world. My work with Dean taught me that such acknowledgment allows for such traumatised patients to then feel more able to accept interpretations based upon what they are doing to the external world, encapsulated in the transference to their psychotherapist. Because trauma is often so deeply felt, and leaves patients dissociated or fragmented, seeking evidence of its presence needs keen observation. Here the paper discusses an experience of bodily countertransference that alerted me to the location of Dean’s trauma’s registration in our relationship. Overall, the paper seeks to demonstrate the importance of psychoanalytic witnessing as a form of containment in itself, and the essential basis for psychotherapeutic work using symbolisation and the transference.

This paper describes the mother–child assessment of a five-year-old girl suffering from anorexia since weaning, which was carried out in an Italian NHS neuropsychiatric child and adolescent unit. The author aims to show how she was able to link the little girl’s refusal of food to a death in the maternal family, which occurred soon after her birth. As well as this post-traumatic formulation, the author links the child’s anorexia to two related aspects of the family dynamics: avoidance of the awareness of death and the inability to manage triangular relationships, due to important intrusion and exclusion anxieties. Using extracts from the sessions, the author shows how the little girl was able to begin to work through the death phantasy which was previously inaccessible to her and her family. adolescence, puberty, psychic isolation, bodily symptoms, separation, individuation, symbolisation, containment, cutting, anorexia

This paper examines psychic isolation as an important element of adolescent development. The author conceives of psychic isolation in adolescence as an affective state with important developmental underpinnings. The affective elements are estrangement and loneliness. The developmental underpinnings include shifting (conscious as well as unconscious, internal as well as external) object relations and senses of the self. Psychic isolation combined with the intensity of adolescent experience can leave adolescents unable to articulate their experience. This difficulty with articulation and symbolisation can leave them vulnerable to breakdown into concrete bodily symptoms. The paper uses Bion’s conceptualisation of containment and the balance of psychotic vs. non-psychotic integrative parts of the personality to examine the emergence of concrete bodily symptoms in adolescence. At times, the transitional space of an analysis, where new experiences can be dreamed together with the analyst, allows adolescents to feel they are no longer ‘unjoined persons’ but ‘members of the wedding’.

Maria Rhode

Maria Rhode

London
UK
Department of Children & Families

Maria Rhode   *Email: mrhode@tavi-port.nhs.uk
adhesive resonance, countertransference, meaning, paralysis of thought, projective identification

Children with autism can have a paralysing effect on the clinician’s capacity to associate freely: connections that seem obvious on reflection may be impossible to notice in the child’s presence. The author argues that this situation can be reached by more than one pathway, and that the degree of the child’s bodily and emotional cohesion is an important factor. Children may seek to immobilise the therapist’s thought processes through projective identification, whether to communicate their own experience of paralysis or because these thought processes are equated with a parental intercourse that produces a ‘baby’ (as described by Bion and Britton). Vignettes are offered to illustrate how the therapist may be nudged into overlooking this baby as well as a potentially growing part of the child that is identified with it, with important consequences for development. A second possible pathway appears to involve the much more primitive mechanism of adhesive identification, in which the child’s sense of continuing existence depends on sticking to the therapist’s surface and any movement can lead to a sense of bodily disintegration. In the clinical illustration, the therapist felt physically constrained and unable to recognise links in the material: it is suggested that this was in resonance with the child’s fear that movement, whether physical or mental, meant losing parts of his body and must be avoided at all costs. These levels can mask each other, and it seems essential to attend to both in order to avoid impasse or the overlooking of essential aspects of the child’s experience.

‘And when you were a child?’: how therapists working with parents alongside individual child psychotherapy bring the past into their work

Claire Whitefield and Nick Midgley

Nick Midgley

Bromley
UK

Nick Midgley  

parent work, psychodynamic child psychotherapy, parenting, early childhood experience, IMPACT-ME, process research, Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis

When a child is offered psychotherapy, it is common that regular meetings will be offered to the parents. However, there are debates in the literature about the degree to which such parent work should include a focus on the parents’ own childhood experiences. This study aimed to examine the way that those offering parent work as part of a study evaluating the treatment of adolescent depression dealt with this issue in their work with parents, both in the study and in routine clinical practice. Design: five therapists were interviewed on the subject of working with parents’ childhood experiences within parent work parallel to child psychotherapy. Data were analysed qualitatively, using Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis. Findings: participants described the need to consider the different parameters of this work to individual adult therapy; in addition, participants felt that it was necessary to negotiate permission to work on the parents’ childhood experiences. They also spoke of making use of insight into the repetition of the parents’ history, the analysis of parental projections and offering containment within the relationship; this varies from the ‘transference work’ of individual therapy and a different style of interpretation was described. Conclusions: there is a need to give more attention to the neglected field of working with parents alongside individual child psychotherapy, especially at a time when such work is under threat within many public services. There are particular technical issues related to work with parents’ own childhood histories that are different to how one might work in individual therapy with a parent.

The development of an evidence-based treatment: Regulation-Focused Psychotherapy for Children with externalising behaviours (RFP-C)

Tracy A. Prout , Emma Gaines , Lindsay E. Gerber , Timothy Rice and Leon Hoffman

Leon Hoffman

Bronx
NY
USA

Leon Hoffman  

evidence-based practice, psychodynamic psychotherapy, implicit emotion regulation, defences, child and adolescent psychotherapy

There is a critical need for the development, evaluation and implementation of evidence-based psychodynamic treatments for children and adolescents. Currently, there are no empirically supported, manualised psychodynamic treatments for children and adolescents with disruptive behaviour problems. The field of manualised psychodynamic treatments with measurable equivalence or superiority to other established forms of psychotherapy is in its nascent stage. This paper details a novel, manualised, time-limited psychodynamic treatment approach for children who manifest disruptive behaviours and emotional dysregulation. Regulation-Focused Psychotherapy for Children (RFP-C) conceptualises children’s disruptive and acting out behaviours as expressions of maladaptive emotion regulation. Externalising symptoms are conceptualised as attempts to defend against painful emotions and thus protect the child from disturbing feelings such as sadness, shame and guilt. This paper provides the theoretical basis for the treatment approach and through the use of a clinical example demonstrates the systematic application of RFP-C in a single case.

[[RunningHead]]

Give sorrow words: working with a dying child

Judith Edwards

Judith Edwards

London
UK

Judith Edwards   *Email: judith@judithedwards.co.uk

What an extraordinary book this is. Now in its third edition, the book arrives garlanded with well-deserved praise from those in our own and related professions, and all people involved in working with dying patients, whether children or adults, are enjoined to read it. While treatments may have evolved and changed somewhat, Judd’s book addresses the fundamental issue surrounding ‘the worst fears anyone with a child can imagine’ as Claudia de Campos says in her new introduction to the book. And of course the worst fears of any child too. This introduction is a significant new feature of the book this time round. It brings us up to date both with the changes of hospital care for children and their parents, as well as with significant advances in paediatric oncology. De Campos interviews an array of policy makers and practitioners, addresses the increasingly interlocking skills available in multidisciplinary teams, and deals with the explosion of information now available through the internet, and its impact on parents and families.

‘I do not have words to express the sorrow’ – Judd quotes Mandela at the beginning of her first chapter, as well as Freud’s words that while acute mourning may fade over time, ‘we also know we shall remain inconsolable’. Yet Judd struggled mightily at times, berates herself in hindsight for not doing enough (and maybe this is something we would all do in these harrowing circumstances), but did find the words. When you are losing a child, how can any death be called ‘a good death’? Is the child allowed the right to be depressed, to be angry or does he or she have to join in the often manic denial that this life is close to its end? At her last meeting with seven-year-old ‘Robert’ before he dies, he screams ‘I don’t want Mrs Judd to go!’ He did not want to let go of a mind which carried on processing meanings, however painful, right up to the end. This is a picture of a mind, as Margaret Rustin says on the back cover, ‘working at full stretch’. One of the dedicatees to the book is Robert himself, and his memory. He has indeed achieved some kind of immortality, as the little Plasticene® figure which he made at the beginning of their two months’ work together is on the front cover of this edition. This figure seemed in hindsight to Judd like ‘a little ghost’ – with its bald head, huge eyes and arms either outstretched in resignation or perhaps also, and this is my own thought, in a complicated gesture of both waving and drowning. It might also be seen to have resonances with Munch’s The Scream.

Social defences against anxiety: explorations in a paradigm

Valerie Sinason

Valerie Sinason

London
UK
Clinic for Dissociative Studies

Valerie Sinason   *Email: VSinason@aol.com

This book, carefully edited by David Armstrong and Michael Rustin, owes its origins to a two-day research colloquium dedicated to re-examining Isabel Menzies Lyth’s seminal (1960) paper ‘A case-study in the functioning of social systems as a defence against anxiety: a report on the nursing service of a general hospital’. Collections of papers to appreciate, develop or interrogate an idea that has caused a paradigm shift can be spoiled by sycophancy or repetition and deplete the original source let alone the secondary ones. However, this accessible, thoughtful and richly varied book allows a rethinking of Lyth’s work as well as an appreciation for the applications of psychoanalytic thinking into organisational work.

Isabel Menzies Lyth, a child and adult psychoanalyst and social scientist who died on 13 January 2008, was one of the pioneering founder members of the Tavistock Institute of Human Relations, established in 1946. Her work has continued to aid all working in hospitals as it showed how the frontline work of nurses left them more vulnerable to the powerful projections and pressures that came directly from their patients as opposed to those furthest away in management who were freed from these. Indeed, as a wartime nurse who benefited from Lyth’s understanding once jokingly explained to me, ‘From a management point of view, patients interrupt the smooth working of a hospital!’

Lyth’s work continued to be crucial for child psychotherapists as she showed the importance of parental presence in hospital wards and highlighted the damaging practice of indiscriminate multiple caregiving. In this way, like Bowlby, she was committed to the importance of attachment and key workers for vulnerable children and adults, but her main and continuing influence both in her lifetime and following her death has been in applying psychoanalytic theory to the workplace. By understanding the specific impact of the client group on staff and institutions and balancing the impact of internal and external, conscious and unconscious factors, the primary work task could be managed in a more humane and alive way.

The mutism of the mind: child and family therapists at work with children and families suffering with selective mutism

Maria Pozzi Monzo , Sara Micotti and Shila Rashid

Shila Rashid  

single symptom, cumulative trauma, dislocation, disappearance, separation, mourning, countertransference

The study of selective mutism in children who are well-functioning in all other areas of their lives, has featured very little in the psychoanalytic literature. Yet, more and more children from as young as four up to adolescence are being referred with this symptomatic presentation to our public and private clinics. This paper attempts to bridge this gap by presenting a comprehensive literature review and two case histories of children who chose not to speak outside of their family home. The complex family and intergenerational dysfunctional dynamics around issues of trauma, loss, immigration and dislocation, which contributed to the formation of the symptoms of selective mutism are explored. In the first of these two cases, the individual psychotherapy carried on painstakingly by the child psychotherapist began with parent–child psychotherapy; the second one began with family therapy and was followed by individual child psychotherapy with parallel family therapy. Both children, their ‘silent’ parents and families were helped to give thoughts and words to unthinkable events and emotions, thus achieving a better level of communication.

parent–toddler psychotherapy, mother–infant psychoanalytic treatment, parent–child interaction, containment

Many psychotherapists working with infants and parents have extended their practice to toddler–parent therapy. This paper presents such work, developed from a psychoanalytic mother–infant therapy mode. Like other published therapy techniques, it invites both parent and toddler to take part in treatment. Similarly, it also takes into account the specific challenges facing the developing toddler and his/her parents. Here, however, focus is placed more clearly on the therapist’s interaction with the child, in the presence of the parent. This involves addressing the child about what the therapist intuits are the unconscious motivations behind his behaviour in the session. It also implies speaking about the child’s feelings towards the therapist. In parallel, the parents’ emotional attitudes towards the therapist are viewed as vehicles that may further the therapeutic process, once they are spoken about. A suitable metaphor is couple therapy, provided one bears in mind the differences between parent and child regarding developmental levels and motivations for therapeutic work. The paper contains a detailed account of a psychotherapeutic treatment with a two-and-a-half-year-old boy and his mother. Based on this presentation, the author compares his work with that of other authors.

The author discusses four inter-related themes of late adolescence: birth/death throes, oblivious objects, manic defences and the potential for physical symptoms, sometimes in emergency form. These issues will be elucidated through the psychoanalysis of a late adolescent who was bulimic and binge drinking. Though her symptoms were severe, elements of her dynamics are seen as characteristic of late adolescence. The definitive separation–individuation processes of late adolescence are seen as a final death throe of childhood and a birth throe of adulthood. In these death throes, the adolescent can see objects as oblivious. The late adolescent can resort to manic leaps to negotiate passages she feels unready for. Such leaps sometimes take the form of physical symptoms, sometimes in crisis form, as late adolescents separate more definitively than in earlier developmental periods.

Working with adoptive parents: research, theory and therapeutic interventions

Robert Fleming

Robert Fleming

London
UK

Robert Fleming   *Email: Robert.fleming@slam.nhs.uk

There is a need for this book. UK-based child and adolescent psychotherapists in the NHS will no doubt be working with adopted children and their adoptive families. The evidence for the increasing mental health needs of children in substitute care is clear (Meltzer et al., 2003; Ford et al., 2007). In the UK, the usual pathway to adoption is from a period in state care (Rees and Selwyn, 2009). Infant adoption is uncommon. Early adversity and age at the time of placement are probably the key factors in the emotional difficulties of adoptees (Van den Dries et al., 2009). It is certainly true that adoptees are over-represented in mental health clinics for children in both the UK and the USA (Brand and Brinich, 1999; Van IJzendoorn and Juffer, 2006). Child psychotherapy needs to be informed about the specific context of adoption in order to be effective (Barth et al., 2005). With the extensive loss and trauma that most adoption triangles contain, it is important to understand just how complex the work is (Hodges, 2005). Notwithstanding all of the above difficulties, the long- term outcomes for adoption are better than long-term foster care and most research suggests that it is an important and effective intervention for children who cannot remain with their birth parents (Van IJzendoorn and Juffer, 2006). The enormous contributions of the adoptive parents are not without complications. Infertility or the lost potential child can have an enormous impact on the parenting offered by adoptive parents (Kaniuk et al., 2004).

In 12 chapters the American editors of this encyclopaedic book manage to corral 21 contributors to provide a mostly coherent and thorough examination of this topic from a predominantly psychoanalytic and attachment theory orientation.

Chapter One sets the stage from which to explore adoptive parenthood. The psychological characteristics of adoptive parents and their motivation are described. The European and American history of adoption is outlined. There is an interesting but brief presentation of some of the controversies in adoption including the ‘openness debate’, which seems more of an issue in the USA. [In the UK most adoptions now contain some element of openness (Biehal et al., 2010) and since the Children Act 1975 (Section 26) adoptees have been able to receive their original birth certificate at the age of 18.] The issue of transracial adoption is dealt with lightly with references to some research, which suggests that transracially adopted children’s self-esteem is not negatively impacted by the adoption (Juffer and van IJzendoorn, 2007). Similarly, gay adoptive parenting is examined fleetingly with a tentative conclusion that the sexuality of the adoptive parents is not a key factor in the outcome of the adoption.

Robert Fleming

Robert Fleming   *Email: Robert.fleming@slam.nhs.uk

The quality of our work as child and adolescent psychotherapists is only made possible by the background presence of a third person. The supervisor creates a triangular space that facilitates another perspective potentially reducing the enmeshment of the therapist–patient dyad. When Zinkin (1995) wrote of supervision as the ‘impossible 206 profession’, he was referring to the difficulty firstly of the clinician communicating the essence of therapy and secondly for a supervisor to grasp the meaning of this work which involves a third person in another place. Addressing this complexity is part of the challenge of inner world work. Ongoing supervision is therefore an essential part of good clinical practice and the central source of continued professional development (Association of Child Psychotherapists, 2015). During my training I had many wise supervisors who gave me invaluable lessons in how to learn from the patient. These internalised supervisors continue to be rich sources of insight and learning.

The editor of this book is an eminent American psychoanalyst who has written inter alia about object relations theory. The book is a collection of chapters from around the world which aim to ‘… approach task, boundary, focus, and interaction in supervision from multiple vertices – research, analytic sensibility, group process, bodily and artistic expression, and individual teaching and learning in clinical supervision’ (p. xvi).

The first piece is an introductory essay by Imre Szecsödy who has often researched the process of supervision. He writes,

The continuous maintenance of boundaries around the task of supervision, keeping an equidistant position, encouraging the trainees to organise the information, and focusing on the patient-therapist/supervisee-supervisor relationship constitutes a mutative learning situation that facilitates learning, irrespective of the type of learning problems’ (p. 10).

He usefully describes three aspects to supervision. The stationary aspect refers to the management of the learning environment (setting, time, method of payment, etc.). The second aspect he calls the mobile aspect and it refers to the continuous reflection and review of the working relationship between the supervisor and the therapist. Thirdly, the supervisory position in which the supervision frame focuses on the patient–therapist interaction.

Briggs has set his contributors a challenge to explain ‘belonging’ and has held them closely to the task throughout. How does a child taken away from his or her family of origin get to feel a sense of belonging elsewhere? Evidence of his drive towards editorial coherence can be seen in the fact that eight of the nine chapter titles have the word ‘belonging’ in them. All of the authors have unique perspectives on the subject but link back to the editor’s focus. This paper reflects on the technical challenges posed to the therapist by an adolescent who finds it hard to engage in the therapeutic process. This is done through the description of a year of three times weekly psychotherapy with a 14-year-old girl who struggled immensely to begin to ‘think’ about her anxieties about sexuality and separation in her sessions. Despite seeking therapy of her own volition, and being reflective about the links between her state of mind and her family history in the assessment sessions, she remained silent for much of the time after she started therapy, only talking sporadically and mainly expressing her conflict through self-harm. The paper describes the therapist’s difficulties in delivering interpretations when confronted with the patient’s defences against having her internal experience understood. Development in the adjustment of the technique and working through the countertransference are described to show how small steps could be taken towards feeling and thinking together with the patient in the session.
